stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The devastating two-year civil war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions By Wycliffe Muia Published 4 November 2026, 06:07 GMT Updated 2 hours ago An Ethiopian-born American citizen has pleaded guilty to passing highly classified intelligence to Ethiopia, including information he hoped would help target and kill fighters from the Tigray region during the country's 2020-22 civil war. Abraham Teklu Lemma, a former US contractor, admitted sharing dozens of classified documents and photographs with senior Ethiopian officials over more than two years, the US Department of Justice said. "In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security," said US Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Ferris Pirro. The 54-year-old faces up to 22 years in prison under a plea agreement. Abraham had worked as a contractor at the State Department, Justice Department and National Reconnaissance Office, the agency responsible for US intelligence satellites. Prosecutors said Abraham worked with senior figures in Ethiopia's political, military and intelligence establishments between 2021 and his arrest in August 2023.

stories.title: Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated | Patience Akumu
stories.summary: Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu View image in fullscreen Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated Patience Akumu I wanted to be a beacon of black feminist love; my friends and family teased me for being a sellout W e had been together 20 years, had two children and had a customary marriage with our village sub-county two years ago without any real plans for a church wedding. So we called our second ceremony a celebration of love and not a wedding. How else would a self-professed African feminist survive being the centre of a colonial and Abrahamic religious ceremony that also manages to reinforce the most male-centred aspects of African culture? Our invitations came directly from me and my partner Mark, not – as is traditional – from our families, and in the form of a playful gif featuring the song Love Potion from the South African group Mafikizolo, a reminder that this was a wedding on our terms.

stories.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopian Authorities Suspend Independent Newspaper
stories.summary: Ethiopian Authorities Suspend Independent Newspaper Andrys Stienstra / Pixabay (file photo). 3 November 2026 Human Rights Watch (Washington, DC) By Laetitia Bader Government Should Lift Ban, End Attacks on Media In what has become the new normal, the Ethiopian government has silenced yet another independent media outlet. The Ethiopian Media Authority announced in a November 2 Facebook post that it is indefinitely suspending the print and online license of the Reporter , one of Ethiopia's oldest media institutions. Publishing in English and Amharic, the Reporter is also the country's last privately owned Amharic newspaper. Stating that the suspension would take effect immediately, the Media Authority accused the Reporter of violating the country's laws and media ethics by repeatedly publishing content that was against "national interests." The authority added that the outlet published "distorted content that negatively affects foreign investment, tourism, and diplomacy." Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The action is part of the government's ongoing assault on the media and civic space in the country and points toward increasing use of vague claims about " national interests " to shut down any critical reporting. Since 2025 , Ethiopian authorities have banned numerous media outlets , deported foreign correspondents , and targeted local journalists through arbitrary arrests, enforced disappearances, and office raids .

stories.title: Africa: Women Still Shut Out of Power As Gender Bias Undermines Africa's Democracy
stories.summary: Africa: Women Still Shut Out of Power As Gender Bias Undermines Africa's Democracy Pixabay 3 November 2026 263Chat (Harare) By Lovejoy Mutongwiza Discriminatory social norms, unequal power relations and growing gender-based violence continue to undermine women's participation in political leadership across Africa, despite progress in representation and the adoption of laws promoting gender equality, United Nations and European Union officials have warned. Speaking at the opening of a two-day Inter-Regional Dialogue on Advancing the Transformation of Gender Social Norms to Enhance Women and Youth Participation and Representation in Leadership and Decision-Making in Zanzibar, UN Women Representative in Tanzania, Julia Broussard, said women's political representation remained disproportionately low, with entrenched attitudes continuing to influence who gets opportunities to lead. Broussard said women occupy just over a quarter of parliamentary seats across sub-Saharan Africa, while in Tanzania they account for approximately 38 per cent of Members of Parliament. However, she warned that progress in representation had not necessarily translated into equal influence in decision-making spaces. stories.title: Kenya: IG Kanja Denies Police Custody of Missing Tanzanian Activist Twaha Mwaipaya
stories.summary: Kenya: IG Kanja Denies Police Custody of Missing Tanzanian Activist Twaha Mwaipaya Capital FM A police checkpoint in Nairobi (file photo) 3 November 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Bruhan Makong Nairobi — Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja has denied that security officers arrested or detained missing Tanzanian activist Twaha Mwaipaya, even as he faced questions in the High Court over investigations into a wave of abductions. Appearing before the Milimani High Court on Tuesday, Kanja told Justice Alexander Muteti that Mwaipaya had never been in police custody anywhere in the country, distancing the National Police Service from his disappearance. "My Lord, I'd wish to inform this court we don't have the subject in our custody throughout the Republic of Kenya," Kanja said. He also denied knowledge of any arrest involving the activist by officers from the National Police Service, insisting that police could not have removed someone they had never detained. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines However, Kanja confirmed that a report on Mwaipaya's disappearance had been lodged at Ruai Police Station and that investigations were ongoing. The Inspector General's appearance came amid mounting pressure on security agencies to account for the activist, who was reportedly abducted on October 25 in Kamulu, Machakos County.

stories.title: Libya's top religious authority rules against wearing Nike clothes
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Nike clothes are popular in Libya, although many are counterfeit By Basma El Atti Published 3 November 2026 Libya's highest religious authority, the Dar al-Ifta, has issued a ruling banning Muslims from buying, selling or wearing clothing bearing the Nike logo. The ruling, issued by the Tripoli-based institution, states that the US sportswear giant was named after the Greek goddess of victory and that its famous swoosh logo was inspired by her wings. It argued that wearing clothing displaying the logo amounted to promoting symbols associated "with polytheism," or the worship of more than one god. Libya is home to the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, where archaeological remains include a statue of the Greek goddess of the same name. The religious committee also accused Nike of supporting Israel and called for a boycott of companies that back the country.

stories.summary: L'exclusion de l'Afrique du Sud de l'accord de l'Agoa aura «un impact a priori assez limité» La première confédération syndicale d’Afrique du Sud a exhorté ce 3 novembre 2026 son gouvernement à poursuivre ses discussions avec Washington pour sauver un accord commercial (Agoa) avec les États-Unis dont dépendent des centaines d'emplois, dans certains secteurs comme l’industrie viticole ou encore les producteurs d’agrumes. « S'il y a des effets négatifs sur certaines filières sud-africaines, comme notamment le secteur automobile, au niveau macroéconomique, l'impact a priori sera assez limité », estime toutefois un expert. This follows Russia and the United States vetoing each other's proposals to extend the 35-year deployment. The UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) was established in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and support a settlement between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front. The latest disagreement in the Security Council followed a US proposal to renew the mission's mandate while placing Morocco's autonomy plan at the centre of efforts to resolve the dispute. Russia rejected the proposal, arguing that it favoured Morocco's position and could prejudge questions of sovereignty.

stories.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House By Allan Olingo Published 2 November 2026 Updated 3 November 2026 US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027. The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements. He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision. The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.

stories.title: Africa: Strengthening Africa's Outbreak-Ready Evidence Generation Capabilities
stories.summary: Strengthening Africa's Outbreak-Ready Evidence Generation Capabilities 26 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) 26 October 2026; OSLO; -- CEPI's Research Preparedness Program, which aims to strengthen regional clinical trial readiness and emergency evidence generation, today announced up to US$8.2 million in additional funding to the Technical Coordinating Partners leading its West Africa component -- the International Vaccine Institute (IVI) and MRC Unit The Gambia at LSHTM (MRCG) -- to support implementation of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC)'s hub-and-spoke clinical trial model. The funding, announced at a launch event on 22nd October in Accra convened by Africa CDC, African Medicines Agency, WHO AFRO and CEPI, supports Africa CDC's hub-and-spoke network which connects experienced clinical trial research "hubs" to a wider network of "spoke" sites closer to outbreak-prone areas. It is designed to enable faster, more coordinated generation of clinical evidence during epidemics and pandemics, strengthening regional readiness for future health emergencies. The initial implementation will focus on West Africa, before expanding to other regions of Africa. "Strengthening clinical trial systems before outbreaks occur, in regions where they are more common, is critical if we are to generate evidence without delay when new threats emerge," said Dr Richard Hatchett, CEPI CEO . "By supporting Africa CDC's hub-and-spoke model, we are helping to build a better connected and coordinated regional clinical research network -- fully aligned with CEPI's 3.0 Strategy, which has a key focus on strengthening globally connected research networks to accelerate outbreak response and the development of vaccines." Across Africa, multiple outbreaks of infectious diseases occur each year that rapidly spread across communities and borders--many have no approved vaccines to defend against them. The ongoing Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is a stark, current example of such.

stories.title: Roy Moxham obituary
stories.summary: Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books View image in fullscreen Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books Obituary Roy Moxham obituary My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India , a country he visited many times on extended trips. His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company. Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.

"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat. Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system. On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft. Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa , meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare). Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site. “We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
